오늘 챙겨야 할 해외 이슈

1) 미 국채 장기금리의 다년래 고점 근처 지속과 동시에 단기적으로 완화된 연준 추가인상 기대 왜 지금: 10년물 수익률이 약 5.31–5.34%, 30년물 5.68% 부근, 2년물 4.84% 수준 등 장단기 금리가 역사적 고점대에 머무는 가운데, 최근 약한 고용(9월 +2.9만명, 실업률 4.2%)과 재평가로 당장 추가인상 가능성은 낮춰진 분위기다. 이 조합은 달러 강세/약세의 미세 조정, 글로벌 차입비용, 주식 밸류에이션(특히 성장·테크)과 크레딧 스프레드에 동시에 영향을 주며, 추세추종 관점에서 금리·달러·주식 간 상관관계 변화를 점검할 필요가 있다. 2) 유가 변동의 정책·지정학 결합 모멘텀(중동 수출 증가, G7 비축유 공조, 공급 약속) 왜 지금: 중동발 수출 증가와 G7의 비축유 방출/공급 약속 등으로 단기 유가가 완만히 눌렸고(브렌트 약 102달러 언급), 이는 에너지발 인플레이션 압력을 일부 완화시켜 금리·물가 기대·환율에 파급될 수 있다. 동시에 중동 지정학 리스크가 완전히 해소된 것은 아니어서, 공급 측 헤드라인의 지속성(방출 규모·기간)과 역내 긴장도에 따라 에너지와 인플레 민감 자산의 추세성이 달라질 수 있다. 3) 유로존 국채 스트레스와 프랑스-독일 금리 스프레드 확대가 키우는 유럽 리스크 프리미엄 왜 지금: 프랑스 10년물 금리 4.87%(장중 4.99%) 근처, OAT-Bund 스프레드가 150bp 넘게 확대되는 등 재정·정치 우려가 유로 약세와 유럽 크레딧/주식 변동성을 높이고 있다. 스페인 조기총선(11월 29일) 이슈까지 겹치며 유럽 채권·FX에 전염 가능성이 거론되는 상황으로, 달러 수급과 글로벌 리스크자산 흐름에 미치는 간접효과를 같이 봐야 한다. 4) 고금리 환경 속 ‘AI 리더십’ 지속과 자금조달 비용 상승의 충돌 왜 지금: 나스닥/빅테크 중심 강세가 이어지며 지수는 사상/근접 고점이지만, 10년물 5%대와 장기물 5.6%대 금리가 지속되는 가운데 일부 AI 인프라 지출 기업(예: 알파벳/아마존/메타)의 마이너스 FCF와 회사채·대출 의존도가 높아지고 있다. 밸류에이션(예: S&P 500 선행 PER <19배)과 자금조달비용의 균형이 섹터 로테이션과 지수 농도를 좌우할 수 있어, 금리 레짐 변화가 주식 내 스타일·섹터 추세에 어떻게 반영되는지 추적이 필요하다. 5) 연준 커뮤니케이션(의사록·위원 연설)과 노동지표 재해석이 단기 기대경로를 가다듬는 구간 왜 지금: 약한 고용지표 이후 시장은 이번 회동에서 동결 가능성을 높게 반영(일부 보도는 80% 수준)하고 있으며, 직후 공개될 9월 의사록과 월러 등 위원 발언이 인플레 위험 인식과 금리 경로에 대한 단기 기대를 조정할 수 있다. 이는 전구간 금리곡선, 달러 인덱스, 주식·원자재의 동시 베타에 영향을 주는 이벤트로, 포지션 민감도가 큰 구간에서 신호(정책 톤 변화) 확인이 중요하다.

오늘 조합은 위험자산 전반의 일제 강세라기보다, 성장주 중심의 선택적 위험 선호가 살아 있고(QQQ ‘매수’ 유지), 광의의 주식과 크립토는 여전히 중립(SPY·BTC ‘HOLD’)인 채 폭은 좁은 모습을 보여준다. 안전자산 쪽에서는 금과 국채가 꾸준히 ‘매도’로 묶여 있어 헤지·완충 수요가 약하고, 달러(UUP)는 10/1의 단기 ‘매수’ 신호가 곧바로 ‘HOLD’로 되돌아가며 방향성이 뚜렷하지 않다. 원자재는 에너지·농산물·금속 전반이 ‘매도’로 기운 가운데, 최근 며칠 사이 유가와 가스가 동시에 ‘매도’ 국면으로 굳어진 점이 눈에 띄며, 이는 금·채권 약세와 맞물려 인플레이션 헤지 성격 자산에 압력이 이어지는 패턴을 시사한다. 흐름상으로는 10/2에 QQQ가 재차 ‘매수’로 복귀한 뒤 오늘까지 유지되고, 금·채권의 ‘매도’ 기조가 9월 중하순부터 끊기지 않는 등 오늘 스냅샷을 뒷받침하는 동조화가 지속됐다. 동시에 SPY와 BTC가 중립에 머물고 달러가 확신을 주지 않는 점은, 현재 위험 선호가 시장 전반이 아니라 특정 테마에 집중된 국지적 양상일 수 있음을 암시한다.

A renewed inflation impulse from energy shocks could keep gold pressured even as demand supports floors. - Additional demand/support: ETFs in August added 121 tonnes (record holdings) and the PBoC bought 20.2 tonnes in August, underpinning structural demand. Deutsche Bank: Gold Oversold and Underpositioned, 2027 Allocation Environment Will Be More Favorable
finance.biggo.com · 2026-10-05T00:00:00.000Z

Gold price outlook macro drivers analysis (based on Deutsche Bank view) - Core thesis: The current gold market is structurally different from 2021–2022. Positioning is light among active/trend funds, while official-sector and long-term allocators have stepped up, creating a divergence that supports upside when macro conditions turn more favorable. - Key drivers to watch (near-term): - U.S. real yields and rate path: If real Treasury yields peak and the Fed slows its hiking sequence, pent-up active money could return, providing fuel for higher gold prices. - Energy/inflation dynamics: Higher oil prices can lift inflation expectations and long-term yields, pressuring gold in the short term but potentially fueling later demand as yields stabilize. - Oil and geopolitical risk: Geopolitical conflicts (e.g., Middle East tensions) can induce safe-haven demand, yet accompanying increases in oil and inflation can offset some gains. - Structural/backdrop factors supporting a brighter longer-term setup: - Official-sector demand: Central banks are purchasing gold at more than double the pace seen in 2021–2022. - Institutional participation: The breadth of institutional involvement has grown roughly 70% since 2021, expanding the pool of assets available to reserve managers. - Demand vs. speculative positioning: While speculative and trend-following money have reduced exposure, central banks and long-term allocators continue to accumulate, creating a supportive base. - 2027 allocation environment: Deutsche Bank expects the environment for gold allocations to become more favorable by 2027, contingent on: - A peak in real yields and a slower Fed hiking path. - Continued central bank buying and expanding institutional ownership. - A re-energized active-money cycle if macro conditions turn favorable. - Near-term risk watch: - If U.S. 10-year yields remain above 5% or oil-driven inflation pressures persist, gold could face downside pressure in the short horizon. - Oil price shocks and Middle East developments can cause two-way effects on rate expectations and gold pricing. Bottom line: The macro drivers for gold are shifting from predominantly speculative momentum to a more supportive framework anchored by official-sector accumulation and potential revival of active money if real yields ease and the Fed moderates policy. Expect a broader, multi-year upcycle if the rate environment turns lower and central-bank demand remains robust.

October 2026 Investment Outlook - Loomis Sayles
Craig Burelle Global Macro Strategist, Credit · 2026-10-01T00:00:00.000Z

US long-term treasury bond yields outlook (Loomis Sayles, Oct 2026) – key takeaways - Global and US context: Labor markets strong worldwide and healthy consumption support modest global growth. Sticky inflation persists, with central banks likely to keep policy rates higher for longer to gradually rein in inflation. - Yields trend: Longer-term rates are rising globally due to sticky inflation and solid growth. The near-term bond rally is unlikely; a slow drift lower in yields is expected as inflation drifts toward targets, but a meaningful crash is not anticipated. - US debt and policy: Deteriorating US fiscal position is not the sole driver of rising yields. Government debt remains large but manageable in the near term. Cyclical factors (inflation, activity) will largely dictate ranges over the next 6–12 months. - Fixed income outlook: High-quality government bonds are seen as hedges in a downturn, but a major rally is not expected imminently. Expect yields to remain in a higher-range environment; opportunities exist for coupon reinvestment at decent rates. - Credit and income: Credit markets have absorbed AI-related debt issuance; demand remains robust. High yield in the US and Europe offered attractive yields (~8% US, ~7% Europe as of Sept 20, 2026). Income opportunities are emphasized as yields are higher, with potential price appreciation limited by a slow drift downward. - AI and growth tailwinds: AI capex and strong consumption act as supportive forces for yields, likely preventing a meaningful near-term decline in yields. - Risks to watch: Central banks tightening further could reduce risk appetite and increase volatility across yield curves; geopolitical/oil-disruption risks (e.g., Hormuz-related shocks) could impact markets. Bottom line for US long-term Treasuries: Yields are expected to drift slowly lower toward targets as inflation cools, but the path remains higher-for-longer with limited room for a large rally. High-quality Treasuries remain a hedge, while high yield and levered credit offer attractive income in a high-rate environment.

Weekly Market Commentary October 5, 2026
strandingroup.lpl.com · 2026-10-05T00:00:00.000Z

US long-term Treasury bond yields outlook (as of Oct 5, 2026) — key takeaways - The long end faces elevated yields driven by higher oil costs, geopolitics, weak auctions, and tighter policy expectations. Yet Treasury buybacks have limited capacity to offset rising supply and persistent inflation concerns. - Near-term risk sits with the short end: about 22% of debt (roughly $7.25 trillion) is in Treasury bills maturing in a year or less. Rolling over into higher short-end yields (roughly 3.95%–5.50% depending on instrument) compounds refinancing costs and fiscal pressure. - Takeaways from policy actions: the Treasury has expanded long-end buybacks (to at least $4–6 billion per operation in 10–30 year space) to support market liquidity, with some initial stabilization in yields followed by renewed volatility when oil or inflation surprised. - Supply dynamics: annual 10-, 20-, and 30-year issuance about $924 billion; even doubled buybacks would only absorb ~14% of new supply, leaving a large supply tail to pressure long-end yields. - Inflation risk remains central: cap on long yields is constrained while inflation runs above target and Fed policy stays restrictive. Fiscal dominance (where fiscal needs outrun price stability) could weaken the dollar and lift inflation expectations. - Tactical guidance for investors: be cautious with 20–30 year bonds due to higher sensitivity to fiscal stress and policy moves; prefer higher-quality names and ladders to reinvest at higher rates; maintain inflation protection; expect ongoing “higher for longer” with a focus on the front end anchored to the Fed, while the long end remains vulnerable to supply and policy experimentation. Bottom line: The longer end is vulnerable to the combination of persistent inflation, rising supply, and limited effectiveness of buybacks; near-term focus should be on the short end’s refinancing risk and maintaining quality exposure in the long end with inflation hedges.

EIA notes inventories near 4 Tcf by end of October (second-highest on record) and rising dry-gas production (~112 Bcf/d in 2026), supported by new pipeline capacity (e.g., Energy Transfer’s Hugh Brinson line from Permian to Maypearl, TX). - Prices have cooled: inflation-adjusted Henry Hub averaged about $2.93/MMBtu for June–August 2026 (roughly 6% below last summer). EIA’s September STEO nudged the 2026 price forecast to $3.43/MMBtu and 2027 to $3.28/MMBtu, with 2027 forecast nearly 29% below the January STEO projection. - Global energy context adds some inflationary pressure but remains moderately insulated for U.S. gas pricing: European/Dutch storage at sub-optimal levels and ongoing Middle East tensions support broader energy price volatility, though spillover effects to U.S. gas prices appear limited so far. - LNG dynamic: The widening Henry Hub–international LNG price gap could incentivize higher U.S. LNG exports, potentially lifting domestic demand modestly and supporting near-term prices if export facilities run near full utilization. - Demand factors: Inflation and higher borrowing costs may temper industrial gas demand growth, offsetting some upside from warm-than-expected heating demand in parts of the Northeast. - seasonal/outlook nuance: NOAA 4-day/short-range outlook suggests above-normal western U.S. temperatures and Florida, with limited early-season heating demand overall; cooler Northeast conditions could lift demand regionally. Bottom line: With record-ish inventories and robust production, U.S. natural gas prices are expected to remain relatively contained in the near term, even as global energy market volatility and LNG export dynamics provide some upward pressure. The price path into 2027 remains soft versus earlier forecasts, driven by ample supply and moderating demand under higher financing costs.

This supports a mixed price outlook with limited directional clarity. - Key regional drivers: - East/Northeast timing risk: ECMWF shows colder conditions earlier on the East Coast (New York City, Boston), which would raise regional heating demand and support higher local prices if verified. GFS suggests a milder East in mid-October. - Midwest spike risk: GFS shows a sharper cold shot in the 11–15 day window (Chicago HDDs higher than ECMWF), which could lift regional cash and basis in the Midwest if realized. - South and Southeast warmth (Houston, Atlanta): GFS maintains late-season warmth, while ECMWF hints at an earlier cooldown in Houston. This divergence can keep Power Burn and wholesale gas markets range-bound in ERCOT/Southeast, with potential for short-lived spikes if ECMWF verifies cooling in these areas. - Demand implications for NG: - Residential/Commercial heating: If ECMWF’s colder East verifies, expect firmer East cash prices and a regional tightening of supply-demand balance. - Power burn: GFS scenario sustains residual cooling demand in the South and Southeast, supporting gas-on-gasoline/ power generation demand in those regions. - Net effect: Despite similar total HDDs (~55.6), the intraperiod divergence reduces the reliability of using aggregate HDDs for price direction. The market should watch the Days 8–15 period in NYC, Chicago, and Houston for potential price moves. - Forecast confidence: Low. Wide intraday temperature spreads and regional timing differences reduce the reliability of a single price direction. Treat macro NG as sensitive to the verification of ECMWF’s colder East and GFS’s late Midwest cold shot. - Data caveat: Based on surface inputs from GFS Seamless vs. ECMWF IFS 0.25°, without ensemble probabilities or urban heat island adjustments. Use with caution for risk management and pricing decisions. Bottom line: Expect a cautious, range-bound macro NG price outlook through mid-October, with upside risk if ECMWF's colder East materializes (boost in East/Northeast heating demand) and downside risk if GFS’s late Midwest cold shot and continued Southern warmth prevail. Avoid relying on the aggregate HDD total alone; monitor the 8–15 day window, especially NYC, Chicago, and Houston forecasts.

Summary tailored to your query: base metals price outlook and macro analysis (copper, aluminum, zinc) - Macro backdrop: U.S. rates repriced lower in the past week, with weaker labor/consumption signals pulling back Fed tightening expectations (October hike probability ~22%). StoneX maintains a base case of one Fed hike in December, but cautions against overreacting to payroll softness. - U.S. demand implications: Slower payroll growth and softer consumer data weigh on near-term metals demand in the U.S., potentially easing upside for base metals prices in the near term. - China view: China remains the key driver. Official manufacturing PMI above 50, services expanding, and construction returning to growth support a constructive medium-term base metals backdrop. July likely a trough for Chinese growth. Supporting factors include mortgage subsidies, lower financing costs, expanded investment quotas, and accelerated fiscal spending. - Inflation and costs risk: Rising factory-gate input costs (energy-related) remain a risk for metals margins, potentially weighing on price momentum if not offset by demand. - Supply dynamics (copper, aluminum, zinc): - Copper: Negative treatment charges and thin stocks imply upside risk from supply tightness, even as macro headwinds (dollar strength, softer China demand) persist. - Aluminum: LME stocks near multi-year lows suggest supply constraints could support prices, though demand softness in some regions tempers magnitude. - Zinc: Tightening supply outside China (e.g., Trafigor and smelter dynamics) supports prices even with cautious macro signals. - China demand softness: Soft credit growth and limited stimulus mute domestic consumption, though pre-holiday restocking has kept copper premiums elevated (highest since 2021), hinting at potential near-term price resilience in the copper complex despite underlying weakness. - Risks to outlook: Elevated energy prices and Middle East tensions pushing factory-gate inflation higher, continued eurozone political strain, and mixed developed-market demand could cap upside and keep volatility elevated. Bottom line: Near term, macro shifts (U.S. rate expectations) suggest modest downside for base metals, but China’s improving activity and ongoing supply tightness—especially for copper and aluminum—provide potential for a constructive medium-term price path. Copper remains most sensitive to supply constraints and Chinese demand cues; aluminum and zinc are supported by stock/availability dynamics and regional supply tightness, though tempered by macro headwinds.

StoneX TV: What Base Metals Tightness Means for Copper Smelter Margins
Natalie Scott-Gray · 2026-09-30T00:00:00.000Z

StoneX TV discusses how base metals outlook hinges on supply rather than broad macro trends. Key points for copper, aluminum, zinc: - Copper: Negative treatment charges and thin refined-stock availability imply tighter upstream margins for copper smelters, even as U.S. dollar strengthens and Chinese demand remains soft. Upstream risks include wage talks at BHP’s Escondido (Escondida) mine. - Zinc: Trafigura highlights a tighter zinc supply outside China due to issues like Budel smelter operations. - Aluminum: LME aluminum stocks are near their lowest since early 2025, signaling potential supply tightness. - Nickel: Indonesian drought is reducing nickel pig iron output even as global nickel inventories stay at record highs. - Broader theme: Supply-side constraints in copper, zinc, aluminum, and nickel are outweighing macro headwinds, shaping the price outlook more than macro factors. Overall takeaway: Short-to-medium term price dynamics will be driven by smelter constraints and regional supply disruptions rather than simply macro demand signals.

Fastmarkets Base Metals Market Update | Sept 2026 - Fastmarkets
Fastmarkets Metals · 2026-09-30T11:00:17.000Z

Summary: Copper - Near-term outlook: Tightness remains outside the US, with LME copper stocks and physical tightness fluctuating. August inflows eased some pressure, but Three-Month LME copper has cleared January highs and could rally toward $15,000/tonne, potentially a blow-off top. - Key drivers: Falling treatment and refining charges (TCRCs) compress smelter margins, risking refined production cuts and further stock drawdowns, which could lift prices and backwardation. A super El Niño could tighten supply further. - Risks: Macro headwinds loom—rising yields, gold and crypto prices suggest risk-off sentiment; equity sell-offs could depress copper. Aluminium - Global supply tightness expected to persist in 2026. - Sector dynamics: Recovery at Gulf smelters is pivotal to restoring pre-disruption output in H2 2026. Geopolitical and operational recovery timing remain key risks. - US-Canada trade tensions: Onshoring and tariffs support domestic primary aluminium, with certain smelters (e.g., Century Aluminum’s Mt. Holly, Magnitude 7’s New Madrid) moving back toward higher production. External supply remains important until new capacity comes online; EGA-Century project in Oklahoma is anticipated. - Market backdrop: LME aluminium supported by tight physical markets, low inventories, and ongoing disruptions; dip-buying is expected to persist through 2026. Zinc - Price setup: Approaching a critical level near $4,000/tonne. A sustained break above could unlock the next rally leg; failure could trigger a sharp correction. - Supply risks: El Niño and diesel shortages raise upside risk. Low zinc stocks mean supply disruptions could quickly tighten backwardation and spike prices. - Chinese role: Exports may ease near term, but weak margins, low treatment charges, and winter power constraints raise the risk of Chinese smelter curtailments, keeping refined supply tight. - Sentiment: Bullish but guarded; prices above $4,000 need to hold to establish a firmer base amid rising supply risks. Overall macro context - Base metals are being driven by a mix of supply tightness, expected recoveries in disrupted smelters, and policy-driven demand dynamics. While copper and zinc show upside potential on tightness and demand, macro headwinds (rates, risk appetite) could cap gains. Aluminium remains structurally tight with regional supply developments and trade policies shaping the near-term path.

Gold declines on still high real yields, with jobs data mixed, Australia's Office of the Chief Economist's significant changes to metals price and market balance forecasts
Ben McGregor · 2026-10-05T00:00:00.000Z

Summary tailored to your query: base metals copper, aluminum, zinc price outlook and macro context - Copper: AOCE raises its 2026E–2031E forecasts to roughly US$6.0/lb (from about US$5.5/lb previously), reflecting reduced anticipated surplus (2025 surplus ~651k tonnes down to ~249k in 2026E) and ongoing supply disruptions (Grasberg, Kamoa-Kakula, El Teniente, Cobre Panama). World Bank copper forecast upgrades for 2026 have continued into AOCE 2026E, supporting a supportive macro view for copper into the mid-late 2020s. - Aluminum: WB’s 2026 price revised higher to US$3,200/tonne in April 2026 due to Middle East supply risks; AOCE has incorporated this by mid-2026 and projects prices to trend down from a peak this year (roughly US$3,387/tonne) to about US$3,076/tonne by 2030E. Deficit expectations shrink from 1,316k tonnes in 2026E to 680k in 2027E and 200–300k from 2028E–2031E, supporting a milder downside pressure into the late 2020s. - Zinc: The World Bank boosted 2026 zinc to US$3,000/tonne (from US$2,750) amid tighter supply and lower inventories; AOCE lifts 2026E zinc to US$3,452/tonne (up from US$3,291 in June 2026) and increases 2027E–2029E forecasts. Despite these gains, AOCE still foresees a downtrend beyond 2026, with prices easing into 2027–2029. - Macro considerations: The AOCE’s revisions indicate a shift to a tighter near-term metal market balance (especially for copper), offset by a slower-than-expected normalization in supply disruptions. This supports higher near-term base-metal prices (especially copper) with a gradual downtrend into 2027–2031. Aluminum and zinc show near-term strength driven by deficits or supply risks, but AOCE projects easing deficits and tempered price paths beyond the mid- to late-2020s. Gulf production recovery falters, China steps up as OCBC raises aluminium forecast to $3,150
www.alcircle.com · 2026-10-05T00:00:00.000Z

Summary tailored to your query (base metals price outlook, with a macro angle on copper, aluminum, zinc): - Aluminium price outlook: OCBC raises its end-2026 price forecast to about USD 3,150/tonne from USD 3,050, citing a slower-than-expected Gulf production recovery. They still expect prices to ease gradually toward 3,150 by Q4 2026, with no strong catalyst through early 2027. - GCC production and supply: Aluminium output in the Gulf Cooperation Council has slowed, growing only ~2% MoM in August (down from 6.2% in July) due to ongoing disruptions tied to the Middle East conflict. The restart of Gulf production remains uncertain, creating upside risk to near-term prices if the situation worsens. - Chinese supply offsetting Gulf disruptions: China remains the key offset, with robust production and continued high exports of unwrought aluminium and products. August Chinese output rose 4.7% YoY (up from 3.1% in July). Exports growth remained strong (unwrought/aluminium products +17.3% YoY in August, vs 18.7% in July). - Market mechanics and spreads: LME three-month aluminium price around USD 3,214/tonne in late September, about 2% above OCBC’s forecast. The cash-to-three-month contango (~USD 7.40/tonne) indicates limited near-term urgency for metal inflows despite falling global inventories. - Price path and catalysts: OCBC’s base view remains that prices will moderate gradually from current levels as Gulf production gradually returns and Chinese supply remains robust. Key upside risk is further Gulf production deterioration or a slower restart; downside risk includes a faster Gulf recovery or weaker global demand. - Implications for copper and zinc (macro lens): - Copper: The report centers on aluminium, but the macro signal—offsetting supply from a large consumer (China) against a slower Gulf restart—parallels copper: China’s strong consumption and refined copper usage could cushion any regional supply disruptions; watch for changes in Chinese demand and electricity costs as primary macro drivers. - Zinc: Similar dynamics apply—regional supply constraints (GCC for aluminium, potential counterparts for zinc) could support near-term prices, while improving Chinese production and demand could cap gains. Global inventories and energy costs remain key levers.
